about: Strings in this repository that look like credentials and are not.
`scripts/secret-scan.mjs` fails the build on anything it recognises as a
credential. Every exception lives here and nowhere else -- there is
deliberately no inline `secret-scan:allow` comment, because an inline mute
needs no justification, travels with the line it excuses, and gets copied
along with the pattern it was written for.
Fields, all required, all strings:
rule      the rule id the scanner printed
path      the file, exactly as git lists it
sha256    SHA-256 of the *matched text*, which the scanner prints next to
every finding so that nobody has to paste a credential into a
terminal or a commit message to write an entry for it
reason    why this is not a secret. Prose, and long enough to be a
justification rather than a restatement of the finding -- the
scanner rejects anything under 80 characters. Describe the value,
never quote it: this file is read by the scanner like every other,
so a reason that spells out the string it excuses makes the
allowlist itself a finding. Write it for the person who has to
decide whether it is still true.
reviewed  the date that reasoning was established (YYYY-MM-DD)
reviewer  who made the call
There is no `expires` field, unlike the advisory allowlist beside it. An
advisory exemption decays because the world moves under it; a "this string
is not a credential" judgement does not decay with time. It decays when the
string changes, and `sha256` already detects that exactly: an entry excuses
one known value at one known path, so replacing that value with a real
secret in the same field of the same file brings the finding straight back.
That is why entries are never written against a path alone.
Before adding one, be sure. A secret that reached this remote must be
rotated whatever happens to the line afterwards -- see docs/secrets.md.

allowed.reason: The KLIPY GIF-search key, and it is a real working credential rather than a placeholder -- which is exactly why it is written down here rather than quietly replaced with `your-key-here`. It is published on purpose: `server/src/routes/media.rs` serves it to every client in the `gif_provider` block of `/capabilities`, the browser then calls api.klipy.com directly with it, and so every network log of every Telium client has always contained it. docs/secrets.md ("Klipy API key") and server/src/secrets.rs both list it as protecting nothing and costing nothing on disclosure. Rotating it would achieve nothing, because the replacement would be equally public; blanking it would break GIF search on a default install, which is the one thing the shipped default exists to prevent. An operator who wants their own rate limit should get their own key and understand it will be equally visible.

The same KLIPY key as the entry above, in its other home: the `Default for Klipy` impl, which is what compiles the reference credential into the binary so that a server with no `[klipy]` section still has working GIF search. Both copies are listed separately rather than by a path glob, because the point of matching on path as well as digest is that a new secret appearing in either file is a finding even though the old one was excused.

Tenor's public web-picker key, in the same category as the KLIPY key above and for the same structural reason: it is exported as `BUNDLED_TENOR_API_KEY`, which means it is compiled into the browser bundle and shipped to every visitor, so it is readable with view-source by anyone who has ever loaded the client. It is a Google-issued key by format, which is why the shaped rule fires on it, but it grants access to the Tenor GIF catalogue and nothing else. `VITE_TENOR_API_KEY` replaces it for an operator who wants their own quota.

The example access key id printed throughout Amazon's own SigV4 documentation, and the most widely published dead AWS credential in existence -- it is used here precisely because the signing test needs the documented key to check its output against the documented signature. Described rather than quoted, because this file is scanned like every other. The shaped rules carry no placeholder exemption by design, so even an obvious dummy costs one entry; that is the intended amount of friction for writing a credential-shaped literal into the tree.

The required AKIA prefix followed by one four-letter word repeated to fill the body, pointed at the MinIO container the backup integration tests start on the runner. It is not a credential to anything that exists outside that container's lifetime, and it is dead on its face: no key issuer produces a body that is one word repeated.

The same literal as `server/tests/backup.rs`, duplicated because the drill test brings up its own MinIO rather than sharing one. Listed separately on purpose: the digest is identical, so an entry keyed on digest alone would excuse this file forever, including a future edit that replaced the constant with something real.

The same Amazon documentation key as the `server/src/backup/s3.rs` entry above, matched inside a revision of this very file. When the two entries above were first written they quoted the literals they were excusing, which put a credential-shaped string into the allowlist itself; a later commit rewrote both reasons to describe the literal instead of quoting it, which is why the working tree is clean. The range scan reads deleted content on purpose -- that is the whole point of scanning history rather than only the tip -- so it still finds the quoted copy in the commit that introduced it, and will keep finding it for as long as that commit is reachable. The literal is Amazon's published example key, so there is nothing to rotate and rewriting history to erase it would cost every open branch a rebase to hide a string Amazon prints in its own documentation.

The MinIO test constant from `server/tests/backup.rs`, matched inside a revision of this file for the same reason as the entry directly above: the reason string that excused it originally quoted it, and a later commit de-quoted it. Keyed on this path and this digest rather than skipping the allowlist file from the scan, because a file the scanner refuses to read is a file anybody can hide a real key in, and the two entries the scanner refuses to read would be the two entries nobody ever reviews. Excusing the exact digests of two literals that are already excused elsewhere in this file gives up nothing: a genuinely new credential written here still has a new digest, and still fires.

`0123456789abcdef` written twice -- the hex digits in order, paired with the matching `api_key = "devkey"` that `sfu/src/session.rs` uses as its test issuer. This file is a local development config for running a LiveKit server out of /tmp by hand; no workflow reads it. A real deployment never has a literal here at all, because Spawn mode generates the key pair when both fields are left empty (docs/secrets.md, "SFU LiveKit API key and secret"), so any high-entropy value appearing in this field in future is a genuine finding rather than another dev constant.

The lowercase alphabet followed by the digits 0-5, used as the handoff secret in the migration dialog's unit tests because the tests assert on the exact string appearing in a fragment. It clears the entropy floor only because it uses 32 distinct characters, which is the honest limitation of any entropy heuristic: sequences are maximally uniform and minimally random. A human can see what it is at a glance, which is the whole reason this file exists rather than a lower threshold.

A throwaway RSA key generated for this file alone, and the reason the FCM tests can run at all. Google's V1 push API takes a service-account JWT, so exercising the provider end to end means signing one, which means a private key; this one was minted for the test, has never been uploaded to any Google project, and authenticates against nothing but the loopback fake in the same file. It is a genuine key in the cryptographic sense and worthless in every other, which is exactly the trade the constant's own comment argues for: a credential in the source of a self-hostable server is a published credential, so the only safe key to publish is one that was never real.

The service-account document the tests write to a temporary directory so the provider has something to load. It is assembled in the test from the throwaway key allowed above, its client_email is on the reserved example.invalid domain which can never resolve, and its project id comes from the test name. What trips the rule is the shape of the JSON rather than anything in it -- the scanner recognises the key names Google uses, and the test has to use those names because the provider parses for them.

An FCM registration token in the shape a real one has -- an instance id, a colon, and an APA91b body -- written so that a reader meets the word fake twice before the end of it. It is a device address rather than a credential in any case: it names where a push goes, it is issued by Google to a handset rather than to this server, and holding one lets you receive nothing. It has to look like the real thing because the test asserts the exact bytes the provider puts on the wire.

An APNs device token, which is 64 hexadecimal characters and therefore always clears an entropy floor no matter what it contains. This one is the sixteen hex digits in ascending order, repeated four times, which is about as far from random as a string of that length can get and is visible as such at a glance. Like the FCM token above it is an address rather than a secret, and the test needs a well-formed one because the APNs path puts it in the request line.
